title: Pointer type and size
concept: Pointers are interpreted differently depending on the type of object they point to.

steps.title: Include stdio.h header
steps.explanation: Header for using ``printf````. ```sizeof``` is not a function but a **compile-time operator**, so it does not require a separate header, but ```stdio.h``` is required to output the result.

steps.title: Start main function
steps.explanation:
Program startup — A **stack frame** of ```main``` is created on the stack. A total of four variables are created here: ````a```, ```c```, ```pi````, and ```pc```.

Key question: ```int*``` and ```char*``` have different sizes of what they point to (4 bytes vs. 1 byte). Are the sizes of the pointers themselves different?

steps.title: variable declaration
steps.explanation:
Prepare values ​​of different types as `int a = 10`, `char c = 'A'`.

These two have different sizes and interpretation methods, and serve as reference data to explain the difference in pointer types.

steps.title: pointer declaration
steps.explanation:
`pi` stores the address of `a`, and `pc` stores the address of `c`.

Both variables are pointers that contain addresses, but when dereferenced, the read size and interpretation method vary depending on the type (`int*`/`char*`).

steps.title: size of int pointer
steps.explanation:
`sizeof(pi)` is the size of the pointer variable itself, not what `pi` points to.

The pointer size depends on the system architecture, and is usually 8 bytes on 64-bit.

steps.title: size of char pointer
steps.explanation:
`sizeof(pc)` is also equivalent to `sizeof(pi)` in the same environment.

That is, the pointer size is determined by the address size of the architecture rather than the target type.
steps.stdout:
Size of int*:  8
Size of char*: 8

steps.title: Reading value with int pointer
steps.explanation:
`*pi` reads the address as an integer according to the `int*` rule and obtains the value 10.

The pointer type determines how the data will be interpreted when dereferenced.
steps.stdout:
Size of int*:  8
Size of char*: 8
Read int*:  10

steps.title: Reading value with char pointer
steps.explanation:
`*pc` reads a character according to the `char*` rule and obtains `A`.

Even for the same address operation, if the pointer type is different, the read unit and interpretation result will be different.
steps.stdout:
Size of int*:  8
Size of char*: 8
Read int*:  10
Read char*: A

steps.title: Program exit
steps.explanation:
It ends with `return 0;` and stack variables are cleaned up.

In summary, pointer size is environment dependent, but type determines dereference resolution rules.

quiz.question: What is the size(sizeof(p)) of `double *p;` on a 64-bit system?
quiz.explanation: Regardless of whether a pointer points to a double or something else, the pointer itself is an 'address' and therefore always 8 bytes on a 64-bit system.

misconceptions.correct:
no.
All pointer variables have the same size.
misconceptions.why: The only difference is the size of the house being pointed to, but the length of the address itself is the same.

keyTakeaway: All pointer sizes are the same, but the type serves as a map to determine ‘how many bytes to read’.
